newsitem.title: UK: Blair to see N. Irish leaders on peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Blair to see N. Irish leaders on peace plan.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair was due to meet key Northern Irish political leaders on Tuesday to discuss new Anglo-Irish proposals which could help break a deadlock in peace talks.

A spokesman for Blair said he would see David Trimble, leader of the province's pro-British Ulster Unionist party, at 0930 GMT, and John Hume of the Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party later in the day.
The meetings follow an agreement reached between Blair and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on the vexed question of the decommissioning of guerrilla weapons.

Bruton, in New York with Blair for a United Nations environment summit, told Irish network RTE that the agreement would create conditions for rapid movement in multi-party talks taking place in Belfast.

Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, has been excluded from the talks because the IRA has refused to call a new ceasefire or to promise to make a start on giving up its massive stockpile of arms and explosives.

Political sources said an Anglo-Irish paper aimed at ending the stalemate between Protestant and Catholic politicians over decommissioning was expected to be tabled at a session of the Belfast talks on Tuesday.
They said it was likely to mirror proposals by the talks' chairman, former U.S. senator George Mitchell, for the issue to be tackled alongside negotiations on other political matters.

Blair said in New York that a possible way out of the impasse had been agreed. "I think it's possible that we have the basis of a way forward. But of course this has got to be agreed with all the other parties," he told reporters.

He said all possible clarification had now been provided to Sinn Fein, which now had to choose between the political path and the dual approach of political action and violence that it had been pursuing.
Unionists were wary of the new Anglo-Irish accord before receiving details from Blair.

"Our concern is that the issue of (weapons) decommissioning will become sidelined," Jeffrey Donaldson, one of Trimble's newly-elected MPs, told BBC Radio in Belfast. Ian Paisley, leader of the smaller and more hardline Democratic Unionist Party, reacted more strongly.
Angry that he had not been invited to meet Blair, he said if the decommissioning issue had been put on the backburner, his party would not attend the talks in Belfast later in the day.
"They (the British and Irish governments) have given in to the IRA. They have said Oh, you can get into the talks without decommissioning at all'," Paisley said.
The "troubles" in Northern Ireland represent one of the world's longest-running guerrilla conflicts, which has claimed the lives of more than 3,200 people over the last 28 years.
